Truly, we shall easily be disentangled from such scruples if we turn our mind to that dispensation of God which I have noted, that he wished at that time to signify and figure both the grace of future and eternal happiness by earthly benefits, and the gravity of spiritual death by bodily punishments, for that time when he was delivering his Testament, still in some way wrapped up, to the Israelite people.

4 The other distinction between the Old and New Testaments is established in figures: the former, in the absence of the truth, showed only an image and a shadow instead of the body; the latter exhibits the present truth and a solid body. And mention of this is made almost everywhere the New Testament is opposed to the Old; yet its treatment is more extensive in the epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There, the Apostle argues against those who thought that the observances of the Mosaic Law could not be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the entire religion. To refute this error, he takes up <margin>Psal. 110. b. 4</margin> what had been predicted by the Prophet concerning the priesthood of Christ. For since an eternal priesthood is bestowed upon him, it is certain that the priesthood was abolished where successors were substituted for one another daily. He proves, moreover, that the institution of this new priest prevails because <margin>Heb. 7. b. 11. c. 19. & 9. c. 9. & 10. a. 1</margin> it is established by an oath. He adds afterwards that in that translation of the priesthood, there is also a change of the Testament. And he confirms that this was necessary by reason, because such was the weakness of the Law that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justices of the flesh which could not make their worshippers perfect according to the conscience, and that it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness through the sacrifices of beasts. He concludes, therefore, that there was a shadow in the very things of future goods, not a living likeness of the realities; and that it therefore had no function other than to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. Here it must be seen in what part the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, the ministry of Christ with the Mosaic. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, a great discord would exist between the two Testaments; but since the state of the question leads us elsewhere, we must aim to find the truth. Let us, therefore, set in the middle the covenant that God sanctioned once, which is eternal and will never perish. The fulfillment of that covenant, from which it finally has it that it is established and ratified, is Christ. While such a confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are as it were the solemn symbols of confirmation. This was coming into contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. These, even though they were only accidents of the covenant, or at least accessions and annexes, and (as the common people say) accessories; yet because they were instruments for administering it, they have the name of the covenant, just as it is accustomed to be given to other <term>sacraments</term> <gloss>sacred signs</gloss>. Therefore, in sum, the Old Testament is called here the solemn method of confirming the covenant, comprised of ceremonies and sacrifices. Since there is nothing solid underneath, unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be antiquated and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the sponsor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification has been acquired once for all for the elect, and transgressions have been obliterated, which remained under the Law. But if you are displeased, take it thus: there was an old Testament of the Lord, which was delivered wrapped up in the shadowy and ineffective observation of ceremonies. And it was therefore temporary, because it was, as it were, in suspense, until it might be supported by a firm and substantial confirmation. But then finally it became new and eternal, after it was consecrated and stabilized by the blood of Christ. Whence Christ, when he offers the cup to the disciples in the Supper, calls it the cup of the New Testament <margin>Matt. 26. c. 28</margin> in his blood, so that he may signify that then the truth of God’s Testament truly stands firm, through which it becomes new and eternal while it is sealed by his blood.

5 From this it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that the Jews were led by the pedagogy of the Law to <margin>Galat. 3. d. 24. & 4. a. 1</margin> Christ before he himself was exhibited in the flesh. He admits that they also were sons and heirs of God, but who, because of their childhood, had to be held under the custody of a tutor. For it was fitting, with the sun of righteousness not yet risen, that there should be neither such splendor of revelation nor such perspicacity of understanding. Thus, therefore, the Lord dispensed the light of his word to them, so that they might see it from afar and obscurely. Therefore, Paul marks this thinness of intelligence with the term childhood, in which the Lord willed them to be exercised by the elements of this world and external little observances, as if by rules of childlike discipline, until Christ should shine forth, through whom the knowledge of the faithful people had to grow. Christ himself marked this distinction when he said that the Law and the <margin>Matth. 11. b. 13</margin> Prophets were until John, and from that time the kingdom of God is evangelized. What did the Law and the Prophets provide for the men of their time? They offered a taste of that wisdom which was one day to be manifested clearly, and they fore-showed it shining from afar. But where Christ can be shown with the finger, the kingdom of God is opened. For in him are laid out all the treasures of <margin>Coloss. 2. b. 9</margin> wisdom and intelligence, by which one penetrates almost to the very inner shrines of heaven.

<summary>Calvin distinguishes between the Old and New Testaments, explaining that the former used ceremonies and shadows to point toward the future fulfillment in Christ, while the latter offers the solid reality of the Gospel.</summary>
